theory.intro: A misleading graph gives a false impression of the data, even when the data values are correct. To explain one, name the feature that distorts the picture and say what wrong impression it creates.
facts: An **irregular or missing scale**, with uneven steps or no numbers, hides the true size of a change.

**Unequal bar widths** can exaggerate a value by area, not just height. In repeated pictograms with a fixed key, full symbols must have equal sizes. When symbol area represents a value, the areas must be proportional to the values.
**Cherry-picked data**, with values left out, misleads by hiding the full picture.
A complete set of mutually exclusive shares of one whole must total $100\%$: each part is counted once. Percentages for overlapping categories or separate groups need not add to $100\%$.
steps: Check the scales rise in equal steps and time gaps are spaced correctly. For bar-height comparisons, check the value axis starts at $0$; a nonzero baseline is not automatically misleading on other graphs.
Check bars have equal widths. Repeated fixed-key pictograms need equal full-symbol sizes; symbols representing values by area need areas proportional to those values.
Check all relevant data is shown. A complete set of mutually exclusive shares of one whole must total $100\%$; overlapping categories or separate groups need not.
Name the feature that distorts the picture and the false impression it gives.

workedExamples.solution_text:
Graph P starts its vertical scale at $80$. Its bars show only the amounts above $80$, making Library B's bar twice as tall as Library A's.

Library B recorded only $88-84=4$ more loans, so it did not record twice as many.

Graph Q starts at $0$, uses equal scale steps and equal bar widths, and shows both libraries. Its similar bar heights fairly represent the similar totals.

The vertical axis starts at $40$, so cutting off the lower part exaggerates the difference in bar heights.

Venue B's bar is also three times as wide as Venue A's. Its greater area makes the sales difference look much larger than $60-56=4$ tickets.

Use a vertical scale starting at $0$ and equal bar widths.

The number of visitors doubled, but the symbol's area became $2\times2=4$ times as large. This makes a doubling look like a fourfold increase.

If symbol area represents the number of visitors, the second square should have twice the area of the first.

The one-year gap from $2018$ to $2019$ and the four-year gap from $2019$ to $2023$ are drawn equally wide.

Membership increased by $20$ in each interval, but the second increase took four years. Equal spacing hides the slower increase after $2019$.

Space the years according to the actual time gaps.

The reported shares total $50\%+45\%+35\%=130\%$.

Each student selected exactly one activity, and all choices are included, so these shares must total $100\%$. The graph cannot be a correct breakdown of this survey.

No. The vertical axis has no numerical scale, so the sales totals and their difference cannot be read.

March's bar is taller, showing more sales, but the graph does not tell us how many more. Add a labelled vertical scale.

foundation.solution_text: The vertical axis starts at $5000$, not $0$. Cutting off the bottom makes Belford's bar look several times taller than Ashby's, even though $5680$ is only a little more than $5280$.
Shop B's bar is drawn much wider than Shop A's. The extra width makes Shop B look far bigger by area, even though it sold only slightly more ($550$ against $500$).
The three percentages are $60\%$, $55\%$ and $45\%$, which add to $160\%$. Shares of one whole must total $100\%$, so these figures cannot all be shares of the same set of A grades.
The vertical axis has no scale or numbers. Without a scale you cannot read the actual sales for any month, so the size of the increase cannot be judged.
No. The vertical axis starts at $0$ and rises in equal steps, and the bars have equal widths. The bars are almost the same height, which fairly shows that the three populations are close.

development.solution_text: The 2021 value ($200$) is double the 2020 value ($100$), but the symbol is doubled in both width and height. That makes its area four times as large, so the increase looks far bigger than doubling.

The years $2014$, $2015$ and $2019$ are drawn with equal gaps, but the last gap is four years, not one. Spacing unequal time gaps equally makes the rate of increase look steady when it actually slowed after $2015$.

Faith sees that Class B's bar towers over the rest. The graph is misleading because the axis starts at $71.7$, not $0$. Every class averaged about $72$, so the real differences are small; Class B is only $0.8$ to $1.1$ marks above the other classes; the cut-off axis blows them up.

Graph P is misleading. Its vertical axis starts at $5000$, not $0$, so Belford's bar looks several times taller than the others. Graph Q starts at $0$, so the bars are almost equal, fairly showing that the three populations are close.

mastery.solution_text: First, the vertical axis starts at $30$, not $0$, so Store B's bar looks much larger relative to Store A's than the values $44$ and $40$ justify. Second, Store B's bar is drawn much wider than Store A's, so its larger area exaggerates the difference. Both make Store B look far ahead of a close result.

Belford's bar looks about twice Ashby's only because the axis starts at $5000$, not $0$. In real numbers $5680$ is just $400$ more than $5280$ — about $8\%$ more, nowhere near double. The truncated axis, not the data, creates that impression.
